meta.description: Not Seneca. Quote Investigator traces this line to anonymous 1955 US newspaper filler — no tie to Seneca, Twain, Gandhi or Ann Landers.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Anger is an acid that can do more harm to the vessel in which it's stored than to anything on which it's poured'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Seneca. It first appears as unsigned newspaper filler in 1955; the acid-vessel image descends from a Turkish proverb.

answer.label: Not Seneca — an anonymous 20th-century saying
answer.authorDates: Earliest documented May 1955, in California newspapers
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traces the exact wording to unsigned filler in California newspapers in May 1955 — the Daily News-Post of Monrovia printed it verbatim with no author. QI found no substantive evidence linking it to Seneca (or to Mark Twain, Gandhi, or Ann Landers, to whom it is also mis-credited). The “acid harms its own vessel” image descends from a 19th-century Turkish proverb, not from any Senecan text.

source.excerpt: Anger is an acid that can do more harm to the vessel in which it’s stored than to anything on which it’s poured.
trail: 1955: earliest exact match, unsigned filler in the Daily News-Post and other California papers — no author named.
Attribution creep: later reprints and quote sites pin it on Seneca, Mark Twain, Gandhi and Ann Landers — none supported by a primary source.
Verdict: Quote Investigator finds no evidence for Seneca and classifies the saying as anonymous, rooted in a 19th-century Turkish proverb.
source.excerptNote: The wording as it first appears in print in 1955 — unsigned, with no author attached.
source.rightsNote: The exact wording first appears anonymously in 1955 newspapers with no identifiable author, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. Seneca’s own ancient works are long in the public domain, but this sentence is not among them.

author.name: Seneca the Younger
author.heading: Who it’s pinned on
author.metaLine: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher & statesman
author.bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was a Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist and adviser to the emperor Nero. He genuinely wrote a treatise De Ira (“On Anger”) arguing that anger injures the person who harbours it — which is why this modern aphorism gets pinned on him — but the specific “acid…vessel” wording appears nowhere in his surviving works and surfaces only in 1950s American print.

misattribution.heading: Who really said it
misattribution.intro: This is a classic “magnet-name” quote: a neat modern aphorism that gets attached to famous sages it has no documented tie to.

items.why: Widely captioned as Seneca because his essay De Ira argues anger harms its bearer, but Quote Investigator found no instance of this wording in his works or in any early source crediting him.
Quote sites such as Goodreads list it under Mark Twain, but there is no substantive evidence Twain ever used the saying.
Both names circulate too, per Quote Investigator; the saying predates or is independent of each and appears anonymously first.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented appearance is unsigned newspaper filler from May 1955 — the author is simply unknown.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Seneca
lead: The sentiment — that rage corrodes the person who nurses it more than its target — is authentically Stoic, and Seneca devoted an entire essay, De Ira, to exactly that argument. That thematic fit is why a punchy, anonymous 20th-century one-liner drifts onto his name (and onto Twain and Gandhi, the internet’s other favourite magnets).

But a resemblance in idea is not authorship of the words. As Quote Investigator shows, the earliest printed instances are unsigned newspaper filler from 1955, and the acid-and-vessel metaphor itself echoes an older Turkish proverb, “Sour vinegar harms its own jar.”
context.pull: The Stoic thought is real; the sentence is a 1950s American paraphrase, not Seneca’s.
